Welcome to **TYPE-ME**, a living resource for methods researchers in health research and psychology. Start with the [condensed version](simplified.qmd), explore the [detailed typology](explore.qmd), or read the [preprint](https://osf.io/preprints/metaarxiv/nyj2p_v1){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## What is methods research?
![](images/logo2.jpg){fig-align="left" width="500px" loading="lazy" alt="A magnifying glass containing research methods, representing the TYPE-ME typology."}

Methods research—research on research methods—aims to develop, evaluate, refine, or provide guidance on research methods, support their implementation or de-implementation, or synthesize existing methods research.[@Schandelmaier2026how]

Methods research addresses methods across the whole research lifecycle: planning, conducting, analyzing and interpreting, reporting, summarizing, evaluating, and implementing research.

Methods research also addresses challenges that require methodological solutions and the consequences of methodological choices.

TYPE-ME focuses on research methods used in health research.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## Why do we need TYPE-ME?
The field of methods research includes many study types, but their definitions, terminology, and boundaries remain unclear.

This lack of clarity

- complicates planning and reporting,
- creates uncertainty about labels,
- limits searchability and indexing in research databases,
- reduces the visibility of methods research as a field,
- obscures what constitutes methodological evidence, and
- hinders standard setting.

TYPE-ME brings these types together as one family and clarifies their similarities, differences, strengths, and difficult boundaries.
:::


::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## How does TYPE-ME organize methods research?
TYPE-ME organizes methods research along two cross-cutting dimensions:

- **Approach:** How do researchers conduct the methods research?
- **Objective:** Why do researchers conduct the methods research?

The detailed typology includes 15 approach types and 14 objective types. One approach can serve several objectives, and one objective can draw on several approaches ([see interactive overview figure](explore.qmd)).

You can characterize a methodological study by pairing approach and objective, much as you would characterize any study by its approach and objective. Three examples:

- A researcher re-analyzes several published datasets to see which of two methods gives more precise estimates: an [experimental analysis of real datasets](approaches/3real-datasets.qmd) (A3) to [compare methods](objectives/8compare-methods.qmd) (O8).
- A researcher runs a Delphi study to identify key items for a new reporting checklist: a [consensus study](approaches/8consensus.qmd) (A8) to [develop a reporting guideline](objectives/10guidance-reporting.qmd) (O10).
- A researcher interviews trialists about why they do not use core outcome sets: a [qualitative study](approaches/7qualitative.qmd) (A7) to [research the dissemination and implementation of methods](objectives/13implementation.qmd) (O13).

For each type, we provide a definition, possible labels, strengths and limitations, examples, and boundary notes where needed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## What can I use TYPE-ME for?
TYPE-ME can help you:

- **plan methods research** by clarifying the study objectives and possible design choices;
- **report methods research** by supporting clearer labels, definitions, and design descriptions;
- **classify methods research** when reviewing a methodological topic;
- **inform indexing and searching** by supporting article types, publication types, index terms, and search filters;
- **define inclusion criteria** for methodological journals, databases, funding calls, or conferences;
- **design programs of methods research** by showing how different types can build on each other, for example from method development to evaluation, guidance development, and implementation;
- **support teaching** by presenting methods research as a structured field with connected types; and
- **identify guidance needs** by showing which types of methods research lack specific guidance for conduct, reporting, or quality assessment.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## How did we develop TYPE-ME?
An international team of 11 methodologists developed TYPE-ME through repeated discussion, written feedback, and testing.

**Team:** [Stefan Schandelmaier](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8429-0337){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Malena Chiaborelli](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2498-0467){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Julian Hirt](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6589-3936){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Anne-Laure Boulesteix](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2729-0947){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Matthias Briel](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2070-5230){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Livia Puljak](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8467-6061){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Zachary Munn](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7091-5842){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Hanan Khalil](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3302-2009){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Dawid Pieper](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0715-5182){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Georg Heinze](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1147-8491){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} · [Richard Hooper](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1063-0917){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}

In two testing rounds, team members independently classified 52 methods research articles from 26 journals, contributing 494 individual article assessments. Testing helped us refine definitions and labels, clarify difficult boundaries, and document remaining disagreements.

Throughout development, we identified published examples for individual types of MR. The examples showed whether proposed types occurred in practice, exposed missing or overlapping types, and helped us refine type descriptions and boundaries, complementing the more formal testing described above.

We will continue to refine TYPE-ME through application, user feedback, and further testing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" collapse="true"}
## How can I cite the typology?
Please cite the typology as follows:

Schandelmaier S, Chiaborelli M, Hirt J, Boulesteix A-L, Briel M, Puljak L, Munn Z, Khalil H, Pieper D, Heinze G, Hooper R. How and why do we study research methods? The TYPE-ME typology of methods research [Internet]. MetaArXiv; 2026. Available from: osf.io/preprints/metaarxiv/nyj2p_v1

:::
